title: Manchester United announce departure of head coach Skinner
description: Manchester United have announced the departure of head coach Marc Skinner by mutual consent.The Red Devils revealed the news via a post on their official club website this morning.The 43-year-old leav...
fullText:
The Red Devils revealed the news via a post on their official club website this morning.

The 43-year-old leaves Manchester United after spending the last five years at Leigh Sports Village.

In his time at Manchester United, Skinner has watched the club enjoy plenty of on-field progress. Under Skinner, The Red Devils got to within a win of a first Barclays Women’s Super League title while the club have been regulars in domestic cup finals. Manchester United won a first-ever major trophy in 2023/2024 as they lifted the Adobe Women’s FA Cup.

A couple of strong league campaigns sent Manchester United into European competition. The Red Devils failed to reach the league phase in their first venture into Europe but last season, the club reached the UEFA Women’s Champions League quarter-finals.

Skinner’s time at Manchester United has produced mixed opinions but nobody can doubt that the club have enjoyed an element of success. The target for a new head coach will be to celebrate success more often and to deliver more regular silverware.

Manchester United are thought to be seeking a quick managerial appointment with the new season now just weeks away.

title: Hughes 'far away' from injury return
description: Hull City boss Sergej Jakirovic says defender Charlie Hughes is "far away" from a return from injury and has "no hope" of making the first game of the Premier League season against Manchester United.  Hughes underwent a hernia operation after last season's Wembley success and complained of discomfort when he returned to first-team training this summer.  "Every player, especially from last season who was a main player in our road to Wembley, to the Premier League, has a big role for us."
fullText:
Hull City boss Sergej Jakirovic says defender Charlie Hughes is "far away" from a return from injury and has "no hope" of making the first game of the Premier League season against Manchester United.

Hughes underwent a hernia operation after last season's Wembley success and complained of discomfort when he returned to first-team training this summer.

Speaking to BBC Radio Humberside about Hughes' rehabilitation, Jakirovic said: "There is a problem and we are trying to solve this problem but it's going very slowly. I think the next two weeks he will still be on an individual programme with the medical team, so no hope for Manchester United.

"Every player, especially from last season who was a main player in our road to Wembley, to the Premier League, has a big role for us."

The Tigers boss was asked if there is a timescale on Hughes' return but replied "too far away."

title: Newcastle Makes Official Announcement Before Matthias Jaissle Hiring
description: Newcastle United’s search for a new first-choice goalkeeper is finally over after months of speculation surrounding the position and a lengthy list of reported targets throughout the summer. The Magpies officially announced the signing of Czech Republic international Lukas Hornicek from Braga on Monday, with the 24-year-old arriving on a five-year contract after Newcastle activated […]
fullText:
Newcastle United’s search for a new first-choice goalkeeper is finally over after months of speculation surrounding the position and a lengthy list of reported targets throughout the summer.

The Magpies officially announced the signing of Czech Republic international Lukas Hornicek from Braga on Monday, with the 24-year-old arriving on a five-year contract after Newcastle activated his €30 million (£25.7 million) release clause.

The Athletic reported the deal’s figures, revealing it would be worth the full value of the goalkeeper’s release clause, which Newcastle activated over the weekend.

Hornicek becomes Newcastle’s fifth first-team signing of the summer following the arrivals of Ewen Jaouen, Bazoumana Toure, Sean Steur and Aladji Bamba. The goalie has already joined the team at Newcastle’s preseason training camp in Spain, with new manager Matthias Jaissle in town but still not officially hired, as no word from the club has emerged since Eddie Howe’s exit.

Speaking after completing the move, Hornicek described the transfer as a major opportunity.

“The last few days have been an emotional rollercoaster from when I first heard about the move and now I’m so happy to be here,” Hornicek said. “It’s a brilliant opportunity in a new league, which I’m very excited about.”

The goalkeeper also highlighted Newcastle’s supporters as one of the attractions behind the move.

“I know Newcastle is a huge football city, with 52,000 fans at St. James’ Park creating an incredible atmosphere and pushing the team every game,” Hornicek said. “I can’t wait to play in front of them.”

Sporting director Ross Wilson believes the club has secured one of Europe’s brightest young goalkeepers.

“His progress in recent years has been remarkable and he has firmly established himself as one of Europe’s top young goalkeepers,” Wilson said. “We knew there would be no shortage of clubs interested in acquiring Lukáš this summer after everything he achieved last season, but it quickly became evident how keen he was to be a part of what we are building here.”

Hornicek played a key role in Braga’s run to the Europa League semifinals last season, helping the Portuguese side finish fourth in Portugal’s Primeira Liga while keeping 12 clean sheets and conceding just 33 league goals. He also earned his first senior Czech Republic cap earlier this year before being included in the nation’s World Cup squad.

The friendly against Manuel Pellegrini's side will be Inter's final test this summer, exactly one week before the opening day of this season's Serie A campaign, which will see the Nerazzurri take on Monza at San Siro at 18:30 CEST on Saturday, 22 August.

The Nerazzurri and the Heliopolitanos have never met in competitive football, but this is their second friendly meeting. The two sides faced off at the Estadio Benito Villamarin in Seville on 17 December 2022, during the break of the World Cup in Qatar. That game ended 1-1, with Darmian responding to Juanmi's initial opener.

title: David Croft praises Cadillac's no-excuses approach after F1 Hungarian GP
description: David Croft has praised Cadillac’s determination to address its reliability problems rather than use its rookie status as an excuse
fullText:
Sky Sports Formula 1 commentator David Croft has praised the new Cadillac F1 team for its resilience and refusal to hide behind its rookie status, following another challenging weekend for the American outfit at the Hungarian Grand Prix.

Cadillac joined the F1 grid as the 11th team in 2026. The General Motors-backed squad, running Ferrari power units with an experienced driver line-up of Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas, arrived with measured expectations, targeting long-term stability rather than immediate points and podiums.

The first half of the season has proved difficult for Cadillac, which has been plagued by reliability problems. The Hungarian Grand Prix was no different. Both Bottas and Perez retired after their brakes caught fire.

During a review of the first half of the season on the Sky Sports F1 Show, presenter Craig Slater suggested that the F1 community is cutting Cadillac 'every bit of slack they deserve because it's the first season'. However, Croft quickly intervened, revealing that the team grants itself no such leniency.

"You can cut the slack, but I don't think they'll cut the slack themselves, and this really impressed me," Croft argued. "I talked to some Cadillac team members on the way home, and they were gutted about what happened with Bottas's brakes in Budapest.

"Another short track, hot conditions, brakes caught fire again. They thought they'd solved the issue, and they're like, 'No, we have got to get to the bottom of this. This is not acceptable.'

"They don't think, 'We're a new team, therefore cut some slack.' They think, 'No, we've got to get on and fix this.' And I love that attitude. That's exactly what you want to see in Formula 1. 'We've got a problem. Get out there and sort it.' So, I hope they do because there are going to be more hot tracks coming their way. Singapore, Malaysia, to name two."

title: 6ft 6in Hornicek part of new cycle
description: Leaky Newcastle kept just eight clean sheets in the Premier League last season and conceded 55 goals, 15th overall with only relegated Burnley, West Ham and Wolves plus Leeds and Tottenham below them.  Newcastle's outfield players clearly did not offer enough protection, but goalkeeper Nick Pope made a handful of significant errors leading to goals while Aaron Ramsdale never fully convinced during his loan spell and has since returned to Southampton.  A new number one was therefore a priority and Newcastle have once again looked to the continent.
fullText:
A rebuild was always on the cards on Tyneside this summer, not least in the goalkeeping department.

Leaky Newcastle kept just eight clean sheets in the Premier League last season and conceded 55 goals, 15th overall with only relegated Burnley, West Ham and Wolves plus Leeds and Tottenham below them.

Newcastle's outfield players clearly did not offer enough protection, but goalkeeper Nick Pope made a handful of significant errors leading to goals while Aaron Ramsdale never fully convinced during his loan spell and has since returned to Southampton.

A new number one was therefore a priority and Newcastle have once again looked to the continent.

The club have mainly targeted players aged 20 and under from abroad, having already recruited Jaouen, Sean Steur, Bazoumana Toure and Aladji Bamba, so Lukas Lukas Hornicek will feel like something of an elder statesman in comparison.

But the Czech only made his breakthrough as a regular starter at Braga 18 months ago and will not have much time to prepare for the physicality of the Premier League.

Hornicek's stature will certainly help - he's 6ft 6in tall - and his ability to play out from the back will give this side something different as a new cycle begins under head coach Mattias Jaissle, whose appointment will soon be formally announced.

fullText:
Ohio State’s reputation as WRU only continues to grow.

With the New Orleans Saints re-signing Chris Olave on a 4-year, $132 million deal, former Buckeyes wide receivers have now earned more than $527 million in contracts in just the last two years alone, on top of having a first round wideout taken in the first round of the last five NFL Drafts — with another one on the way in 2027.

WRU Stackin’ up 💰

— Ohio State Football (@OhioStateFB) August 2, 2026

While Brian Hartline has moved on, there doesn’t appear to be any letting up at the position for Ohio State in the near future.

New position coach Cortez Hankton still owns a stacked room, with Jeremiah Smith obviously leading the way alongside Chris Henry Jr. and Brandon Inniss, transfers Kyle Parker and Devin McCuin and exciting freshmen Brock Boyd and Jerquaden Guilford. That’s not to mention five-stars Jamier Brown and Jett Harrison committed in the next two recruiting classes.

As such, the program’s reputation as a wide receiver factory will continue to live on beyond Hartline, and prospects are keeping Ohio State at the forefront of their mind as a result.

One of those guys is four-star 2028 wideout Hayden Koo, who listed the Buckeyes among his top 12 schools over the weekend alongside Michigan, Oregon, USC, Washington and others.

Extremely blessed to be in a position to have a Top 12! Thank you to all the schools in this process and journey! Also big thank you to @CfbRalb @GregBiggins @ChadSimmons_@BlairAngulo @PGregorian@BrandonHuffman @ocvarsityguy @mikehuntley63 @adamgorney@247Sports… pic.twitter.com/34cT7XUYNi

Koo ranks as the No. 21 WR in the country and the No. 147 player nationally per 247Sports’ rankings, hailing as the top pass-catcher out of his home state of California. The 6-foot-1, 170-pound receiver is coming off a big sophomore campaign, catching 53 passes for 796 yards and seven touchdowns at Tustin High School.

Ohio State offered Koo earlier this June after he dominated one of the first recruiting camps of the summer, getting in ahead of offers from both Michigan and in-state USC.

“This offer is very special,” Koo told Greg Biggins of Rivals. “A lot of people will consider them WRU. In my opinion, the top three would be Ohio State, LSU, and SC. It was huge with what they show in the draft, and just the receivers that they have.”

Ohio State currently has three players committed in its 2028 class, led by the aforementioned Harrison, the younger brother of Marvin Harrison Jr. The Buckeyes also hold commitments from four-star defensive end Jameer Whyce and four-star RB Elijah Newman-Hall. All three guys are top-80 national players.

title: Josh Heupel reveals hard truth about Tennessee football quarterback future
description: It’s plausible that the loser of Tennessee’s QB competition between George MacIntyre and Faizon Brandon won’t return in 2027, and Josh Heupel knows it
fullText:
It’s plausible that the loser of Tennessee football's quarterback competition between George MacIntyre and Faizon Brandon won’t return to the Vols in 2027, and coach Josh Heupel knows that reality.

“I think that’s the era of college football that we’re in,” Heupel said on July 20 at SEC media days. “And it’s kind of been that way for a while now.”

Heupel was responding to a straightforward question about the consequences of naming a starting quarterback: Do you consider that when you choose one, you might also lose one?

Heupel is skilled at eluding such questions. But he instead just acknowledged the reality of college football in the portal era.

Both young UT quarterbacks were highly touted recruits. But likely only one will remain with the Vols long term. And depending on how clearcut one quarterback wins the job, the loser of the competition could go into the transfer portal.

Tennessee starts preseason practice on Aug. 5. Heupel said he’s pleased with the progress of both quarterbacks. But he knows the competition could impact the team beyond this season.

It’s a common scenario in the portal era: Two blue-chip quarterbacks compete for the starting job. The winner stays. The loser ultimately leaves to try his luck at another school.

Heupel has gone through this a couple of times before at Tennessee.

In 2022, UT signed four-star quarterback Tayven Jackson. A year later, Jackson transferred to Indiana because five-star Nico Iamaleava arrived with a clear path to the starting job.

In 2024, UT signed four-star quarterback Jake Merklinger. A year later, Merklinger transferred to UConn because MacIntyre had pulled ahead of him in practice.

It’s reasonable to assume that it could happen again after the 2026 season, but that might depend on how the competition plays out.

Heupel acknowledged that whoever he names as the starter must prove it in games. He recalls when Joe Milton started the first two games of the 2021 season, but Hendon Hooker ultimately took the job and never relinquished it.

That opens a wide range of possibilities.

If by season’s end, the best quarterback is unclear, both could return to compete in 2027. However, if UT struggles through a season-long quarterback carousel in 2026, it might dip into the portal for a transfer in 2027.

If Brandon is the best quarterback in 2026, it’s reasonable to believe that MacIntyre would transfer. That’s what happened when Jackson and Merklinger were overtaken by a younger, higher-rated quarterback.

If MacIntyre is the best quarterback in 2026, Brandon would have to consider how long he might wait for his turn at the starting job. MacIntyre is a redshirt freshman, so he’d be eligible for the NFL draft following the 2027 season. Brandon is a freshman, one year behind MacIntyre.

That’s jumping far ahead. But make no mistake that UT coaches consider the long-term ramifications of any quarterback battle, especially if it involves two young talents with plenty of eligibility.

title: How Alabama football's Bray Hubbard was shaped by mother's cancer battle | Exclusive
description: Don't tell Alabama football's Bray Hubbard about adversity. He was shaped by his late mother's battle with cancer.
fullText:
Those closest to Bray Hubbard know the Alabama football safety doesn’t need much to be satisfied.

“He is so, just, chill,” said Blake Pennock, who was Hubbard's football coach at Ocean Springs in Mississippi. “Put him somewhere, in a deer stand or on a boat fishing, or whatever else. There ain’t a whole lot that needs to please Bray.”

It’s the simple things for Hubbard, Alabama defensive coordinator Kane Wommack said. It’s football. It’s hunting. It’s friendships. In the words of the Alabama football program, that is “keeping the main thing the main thing,” something for which Hubbard has come to be the prototype.

Viewed as a centerpiece of a veteran-laden defensive backfield, Hubbard is seen as the heartbeat of the Crimson Tide, one who sets the tone with his example, his tenacity, his physicality, his nature.

“I mean, he’s just been about his business,” Alabama football coach Kalen DeBoer said. “You could always count on him. He was tough. He was out there practicing, plays on Saturdays, (and) finds a way to make it happen, whether he was in pain or not.”

Hubbard knows who he can be when staring in the face of trial. It’s always been more than physical pain or aches, a missed tackle or a loss in a game.

Affliction has always been bigger for Bray and the Hubbard family, adversity faced well before Alabama football was secured as Bray’s future. This trial, though, this connection to his mother defines who Bray is and who he became for the Crimson Tide.

“When he has some bad things happen or something doesn’t go his way,” said Mark Hubbard, Bray’s father, “it doesn’t affect him because he’s been through real adversity.”

Courtney Hubbard was the ultimate team mom. She loved to yell, scream and cheer, unleashing a high-pitched “woo-woo” on whoever was nearest her.

“Everybody knew that noise,” Mark Hubbard said. “Everybody knew it was her. It was just kind of her call.”

BRAY HUBBARD RETURNS TO ALABAMA: Why Bray Hubbard wants to finish his Alabama football story

BRAY HUBBARD, THE QB: How Bray Hubbard went from star high school QB to Alabama football DB

Courtney, an elementary school teacher in Ocean Springs for 18 years, was a softball player, someone who understood that if Bray gave his all and played hard, she could live with mistakes.

For 8½ years, Courtney fought. At age 31, early in her diagnosis of breast cancer, she would drive 90 minutes to New Orleans to catch the first flight to Houston every Wednesday. She would get her treatment at MD Anderson Cancer Center before flying back to New Orleans and driving back to Ocean Springs to be there for her kids’ nights and games.

The cancer later returned to her bones before metastasizing and spreading to her organs. She died in January 2018 at age 40. Her twin children Brock and Maura Kaye were 15. Bray was 12.

"She was just a fighter," Bray said.

Bray knows about adversity. But it's not in the context of what he's asked about on a daily basis, whether it was a loss to Florida State or a loss to Indiana in the College Football Playoff quarterfinal at the Rose Bowl.

That's not adversity in the Hubbard house.

"Adversity is when you lose your mother, your mother dies when you’re a child," said Mark, who was married to Courtney for 20 years. "That’s adversity. That’s the mentality we have.”

As Mark watches Bray grow up, he sees Courtney.

Mark sees Courtney’s mannerisms in Bray. He sees her humility and kindness. It’s in Bray’s loyalty to his friends, in his eagerness to sign each autograph or take each picture when he’s asked. It’s in Bray’s inability to make excuses or give up, just like his mother.

"He's rough and tough, but, deep down, he's a really good, thoughtful kid that I really think he got from his mom," Mark said.

For Bray, Courtney is not solely a symbol of what true adversity is. She is an example of how to live, how to treat others even when bad days come.

"I think it's just the way that she impacted the people around her and everybody in the community," Bray said. "I try to just be nice to everybody and have a smile on my face wherever I go because that's ultimately what she did."

Courtney's impact stems from Bray and into the rest of the Alabama roster.

“He’s not trying to look for the next branding opportunity,” Wommack said. “He’s not necessarily looking for how to necessarily gain an edge in life. He takes things as they come, and he keeps the main thing the main thing and enjoys himself as a great friend and as a great teammate.”

That is the least Bray can be to honor his mother. If something doesn't go well, she is always on his mind, helping him through.

"She was fighting Stage 4 cancer and you would have never known it, if you didn't know her. You just got to keep fighting. That's what she did."

Colin Gay covers Alabama football for The Tuscaloosa News, part of the USA TODAY Network. Reach him at cgay@gannett.com or follow him @_ColinGay on X, formerly known as Twitter or Instagram @colingaytnews.

title: YMCA welcomes former Big Ten champion as Megalodons head coach

fullText:
Axel Birnbrich head coach of the Muskingum Megalodons Swim Team at the Muskingum Family YMCA

Birnbrich brings more than 40 years of coaching experience to the role, according to a community announcement. The announcement said his background includes coaching in YMCA, USA Swimming, high school and club programs, working with athletes across a range of ages and skill levels.

The YMCA highlighted Birnbrich's competitive swimming accomplishments, noting that he was a Big Ten champion, Olympic Trials qualifier, four-year letterman at Ohio State University and a team captain.

According to the announcement, Birnbrich has spent decades helping swimmers pursue success both in competition and beyond the pool.

The hiring marks a new chapter for the Muskingum Megalodons program. The YMCA said Birnbrich's experience, leadership and passion for swimming will help support the team's continued growth and development.

The Muskingum Family YMCA said additional information will be released about an upcoming meeting for swimmers and parents.

The gathering will provide an opportunity for families to meet Birnbrich, hear about his vision for the Megalodons program and learn more about the upcoming season, according to the announcement.

title: The numbers behind NI's 158 Commonwealth Games medals
description: As the Games in Glasgow come to a close, BBC Sport NI looks at the numbers behind Northern Ireland's 158 Commonwealth Games medals.
fullText:
With 16 medals in Glasgow, Team Northern Ireland surpassed the landmark of 150 medals at the Commonwealth Games.

It has been a successful games for Northern Ireland athletes, and a tally of three golds, four silvers and nine bronze medals in Glasgow to take the overall tally to 158 medals.

It is the second-highest number of medals for Northern Ireland in the history of the Commonwealth Games.

Kate O'Connor was dominant in the heptathlon and boxer Jon McConnell claimed a famous gold medal, while the Games ended with Gary Kelly and Adam McKeown winning the men's pars final in bowls.

There was also success in the ring with further six medals and another four in the swimming pool.

But what are the numbers behind Northern Ireland's success at the Games? Let's break it down.

O'Connor wins NI's first gold medal in heptathlon

Wiffen rallies for silver as McCartney claims bronze

McConnell takes gold as Walsh and Rock claim silver

Why the Commonwealth Games are important to NI athletes

Northern Ireland have competed in all but two Commonwealth Games.

The first edition in 1930, when it was known as the Empire Games, athletes from Northern Ireland participated in Ontario as Ireland, and claimed a silver medal through Bill Britton in the hammer throw, but in this article we will focus on medals won as Team Northern Ireland.

The first medals as Northern Ireland came in 1934 in London, when the men's fours team claimed a silver in bowls, while William Duncan and Jimmy Magill won boxing bronze medals.

After a medal-less 1938 Games and no Northern Ireland representatives in Auckland when the Games resumed in 1950 after the end of the World War Two, the first two gold medals arrived in Vancouver in 1954 - the first year it was known as the Empire and Commonwealth Games.

Thelma Hopkins won the high jump, while William Rosbotham and Percy Watson - remarkably also one of the 1934 silver medallists - won the men's pairs in bowls.

Edinburgh has been a productive city for Northern Ireland in the Commonwealths, and 1970 brought two gold medals for Dame Mary Peters, in the pentathlon and shot put, while Mike Bull took gold in the pole vault.

Sixteen years later, Northern Ireland had their most successful Games up to that point with 15 medals.

Phil Beattie's 400m hurdles win and Freda Elliott and Margaret Johnston's women's pairs triumph in the bowls were the only two golds, but four silvers and nine bronze medals made it NI's most fruitful Games yet.

The 1994 Commonwealths in Victoria set a new Northern Ireland record for the number of gold medals at a single competition with five, as Johnston claimed a singles title, Neil Sinclair and Jimmy Webb won gold in the ring, while David Calvert and the duo of Tom Hewitt and Samuel Allen were successful in shooting.

Calvert would strike again four years later with two golds, one of which came in the pairs event with Martin Millar, and another individual double followed in 2002 in Manchester.

The 2010 Games in Dehli are remembered for a hat-trick of boxing golds as Michael Conlan, Paddy Barnes and Eamonn O'Kane all won, and the former pair became double Commonwealth champions in Glasgow four years later.

Rhys McClenaghan's triumph on the Gold Coast in 2018 was a first gymnastics medal for Northern Ireland and seven silver medals plus four bronze matched the tally of 12 medals from Glasgow.

But it was in 2022 in Birmingham when Northern Ireland had, by some distance, their most successful Games to date with seven gold medals, seven silvers and four bronze.

Aidan and Michaela Walsh, Jude Gallagher, Dylan Eagleson and Amy Broadhurst all won golds in boxing, while Bethany Firth came out on top in the women's 200m S14 and the men's four quartet of Martin McHugh, Ian McClure, Sam Barkley and Adam McKeown were triumphant in bowls.

There were also notable silvers for Daniel Wiffen and McClenaghan, who both would go on to become Olympic champions two years later, while Ciara Mageean and O'Connor, who won NI's first gold in 2026, finished second in the 1500m and heptathlon respectively.

Jon McConnell added to O'Connor's success in Glasgow with a gold in the ring, and the duo of Kelly and McKeown ended NI's Games on a high with victory in the men's pairs final.

In terms of a number of gold medals and an overall tally, boxing is the most successful sport for athletes from Northern Ireland - and by some margin.

Of the 18 gold medals won in the sport, there have been a number of notable names who went on to have distinguished careers.

Barry McGuigan won gold in Edmonton in 1978, Wayne McCullough was Commonwealth champion in 1990, while Barnes is the only boxer to win consecutive gold medals.

The first gold for a NI boxer came in 1958 in Cardiff through Terry Milligan, and it is fitting the landmark 150th medal also came in the ring with a flurry of medals on Friday.

Such has been the success of NI boxers, they have won 49% of all Commonwealth medals.

Bowls is next in line with another successful Games, with Kelly winning bronze in the singles before he pairs gold with McKeown, while Chloe Wilson and Shauna O'Neill claimed bronze in the women's competition.

That takes bowls' tally to 25 overall, six of which are gold.

Neil Booth and Kelly have four medals to his name, while Margaret Johnston and Ian McClure each have two golds and a bronze to their name.

Lady Peters leads the athletics tally with her three gold medals and a silver, and O'Connor's gold in Glasgow was the first in a multi-event since the 1972 Olympic champion, and the first athletics gold since Beattie in 1986.

Northern Ireland have only won a gold medal in six sports, and McClenaghan in 2018 and Firth's success four years ago are the only time in their respective events.

There have been three sports where Northern Ireland has one solitary medal - with Ivan Weir winning middleweight bronze in wrestling in 1978, Janet Yates claimed silver four years later in archery and Chloe McCombe, along with guide Catherine Sands, in the para-triathlon in Birmingham in 2022.

There have also been eight judo medals - two of which came from Joshua Green and Rachael Hawkes in Glasgow - and four in cycling, but none have been gold.

Along with McCombe, Firth and swimmer Barry McClements are the other para-athletes who have won medals for Northern Ireland.

Shooter David Calvert is the most successful athlete from Northern Ireland at the Commonwealth Games, with eight medals - four of which were gold.

Calvert's first medal came at the 1982 Games in Brisbane alongside Hazel Mackintosh in the full bore rifle pairs.

His first gold came in Victoria in 1994 in same discipline and his last was a bronze medal in Delhi in 2010 aged 59, which made him the oldest NI athlete to medal.

Six athletes from Northern Ireland have won four medals each.

Shooter Martin Millar won his two gold medals alongside Calvert, and has two bronze medals to his name.

Lady Mary Peters and Mike Bull both won silver for their first Games medals in 1966, in the shot put and pole vault respectively.

Peters won a shot put and pentathlon double in 1970 - the latter of which she would win again four years later - while Bull was first in the decathlon in 1974 and also added another gold and silver to his pole vault tally.

Michaela Walsh is the first boxer to win four medals for Northern Ireland. She won gold in 2022 to add to her silvers in 2014 and 2018, and claimed a third silver in Glasgow on Saturday.

After his gold on Sunday, Kelly joins fellow bowler Neil Booth on a quartet of Commonwealth medals.

title: Cheers, tears and records for Team Wales in Glasgow
description: Team Wales return from the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow  with 31 medals including nine gold, 10 silver and 12 bronze
fullText:
So there we have it. Ten sports and more than 10 days of action.

Team Wales return from the Commonwealth Games with 31 medals including nine gold, 10 silver and 12 bronze, while sprint cyclist Emma Finucane proved one of the stars in Glasgow.

Finucane showed the success of the Wales women during the past two weeks as they were involved in 21 medals.

Australia’s national anthem appeared to be on a loop with 70 golds as they topped the medal table, with Wales finishing ninth.

So was this a success for Team Wales? Chef de mission Gethin Jones says so, but is he right?

Wales' most successful Games were on the Gold Coast in 2018, where they won 36 medals - 10 golds, 12 silvers and 14 bronze.

These Commonwealth Games in Glasgow cannot be directly compared to the event in Australia eight years ago because there were fewer sports and medals.

This event was a condensed competition after the state of Victoria in Australia pulled out of hosting and the Scottish city stepped into save the Games.

On this occasion, Wales surpassed the 28-medal haul of Birmingham in 2022, although they finished one place lower in the medal table.

Cycling was the dominant sport with 11 medals, with six in swimming, five in athletics, four in boxing, three in artistic gymnastics and one each in bowls and weightlifting.

Team Wales roll of honour at Commonwealth Games

Final medal table as Australia dominate Glasgow 2026

Finucane proved why she is considered a generational talent by rewriting the record books with four golds in four events in four days.

The 23-year-old became the first track cyclist and Welsh athlete to achieve this feat with success in consecutive days in the the team sprint, individual sprint, keirin and 1,000m time trial.

She was rewarded with the honour of carrying the flag at the closing ceremony.

Finucane led a strong Welsh cycling contingent, with world champion Anna Morris not far behind the sprint star in the medal stakes.

Endurance rider Morris finished won two golds and a bronze, while Jess Roberts, Rhian Edmunds and Lowri Thomas and Ciara Oliva also stood on the podium.

Day to remember for record-breaking Finucane

Finucane creates Games history with fourth gold

Finucane was not the only Team Wales member to rewrite the record books.

Matt Richards became the first Wales swimmer to win four medals in one Games, with two silver and two bronze, although the gold medal in both the 100m and 200m freestyle just eluded him.

Richards was the driving force in a swimming squad that won four more medals than in Birmingham.

Team captain Olivia Breen briefly became the most successful Welshwoman in Commonwealth Games history, when she added T38 long jump gold to silver in the 100m. This was before being taken over by Finucane.

There was also the wonderful moment Ciara Oliva managed a bronze in the women's team pursuit.

Oliva and her husband Lewis had both come out of retirement after having three children.

Weightlifter Laura Hughes also won bronze eight years on from the same medal she achieved in Australia.

Boxer Rosie Eccles will hang up her gloves after completing the set of medals with her bronze.

Eccles had some choice words for some of her critics in her post-match fight where she also insisted she would not reverse her retirement decision, saying she "had a full heart but empty tank".

Finucane‘s fourth podium position will be among Wales’ defining moments of the Games but will be rivalled by the first gold.

Not just because it was the first time Wales had topped the podium and heard the national anthem, but because of the manner in which Ruby Evans achieved it.

The Welsh gymnast had suffered disappointment with her team-mates by finishing fourth in the team competition.

That was compounded in the all-around individual event when a poor balance beam routine saw her fall off and effectively ended her medal hopes. She ended up sixth.

Evans finished the competition in tears and you wondered whether that would be her defining image in Glasgow.

The Cardiff gymnast sat out the following day as identical twins Emily and Abigail Roper won bronze medals on different apparatus within the space of two hours.

Evans then returned with a brilliant floor routine that delivered gold.

Expectation surrounding the Olympian was intense before the Commonwealth Games and she delivered under pressure. From despair to delight within 48 hours.

The inclusivity of these Games has often been highlighted and the Para-sport influence has again been strong in Team Wales, with 10 medals to show for their efforts.

Para-swimmer Ela Letton-Jones started the ball rolling by winning Wales' first medal on the opening night, with Rhys Darbey later joining her on the podium.

Breen and Aled Davies led the way in athletics with gold, while discus throwers Funmi Oduwaiye and Bree Cronin also chipped in with medals.

Para-cyclist James Ball and his pilot Matt Rotherham had to settle for two silvers as they could not overcome home hero Neil Fachie.

Then there was the Para-bowls mixed pair of Steffan James and Julie Thomas who claimed bronze.

They were guided by Jamie Jones and John Wilson, who at 72 was the oldest Team Wales member to stand on the podium in these Games.

Thomas, who lost her sight before taking up bowls, provided one of the most heartwarming moments of the Games.

Or more specifically her faithful guide dog Yoko did when she was awarded a costume for the closing ceremony.

There might have been no medals but there was a welcome debut for the 3x3 wheelchair basketball teams.

The Welsh Para-athletes delivered again as they accounted for all five of the track and field medals.

It was the second successive Games n which an able-bodied athlete did not finish on the podium in track and field, with fourth-place finishes for Jake Heyward and Charlotte Henrich in the men's mile and women's 400m respectively.

Sprinter Jeremiah Azu could not improve on his fifth place from four years ago in a world-class 100m raced in atrocious conditions.

Welsh Athletics will point to the fact that 15 of the 18 athletes who competed achieved top-six placings, but they will want some podium positions in India in four years.

Boxing had a decent return of medals with four podiums from the seven-strong team, including silvers for Orlando Holley-Sotomi and Connor Williams, but they will be disappointed to be leaving a Games without a gold for the first time since 2014.

There will also be an inquest into the Welsh netball set-up after they finish 10th out of 12, two places lower than the eighth they managed at Birmingham 2022, after just one win from their six games, while there were no medals for judo.

There are also the moments of drama and near misses you associate with major events.

The velodrome provided one, with Ioan Hepburn being led away from the track distraught before the men's team sprint bronze medal race because he was unable to compete because of illness with Wales unable to compete in the race.

The following day Morris was denied a silver medal in the scratch race, which took place just an hour after her individual pursuit success, when she was demoted from second to fifth.

The Indian city of Ahmedabad will host the next event in 2030 after Glasgow kept the Commonwealth Games alive.

It will represent the 100th birthday of the Games and it will be interesting to see how the future of the event fits into the modern sporting calendar.

While stuck in the bubble of Glasgow 2026, there is the realisation this was a stripped back Games, even though the positive stance would be to call it "reimagined".

The challenge always is for the sports now is to try to maintain profile following a competition that is battling to stay relevant.

Chef de mission Jones says "we need everyone to get behind Team Wales over the next four years".

Then we will do it all again in India in 2030.

'No guarantees' - joyful Glasgow cannot banish all Commonwealth doubts

title: Wales first nation to withdraw support for Infantino
description: Wales become the first nation to publicly withdraw backing for Gianni Infantino's bid to continue his leadership of Fifa.
fullText:
Wales have become the first nation to publicly withdraw backing for Gianni Infantino's bid to continue his leadership of Fifa.

It follows the loss of confidence in the Fifa president following his scrapped plans to sell stakes in its competitions to private investment firms.

The Football Association of Wales (FAW) has confirmed "its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Mr Gianni Infantino for re-election as Fifa president for the 2027-2031 term".

Infantino's lucrative plan sparked a global outcry, with European football's governing body Uefa threatening to boycott all Fifa competitions, including the World Cup.

Uefa and Concacaf - which oversees football in North, Central America and the Caribbean - both released statements on Saturday criticising the leadership of the world governing body following Infantino's decision to withdraw the plan.

The FAW added: "The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgement have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football.

"Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept."

title: Was Glasgow a successful Games for Team Scotland?
description: How do you assess the success of Team Scotland after the 2026 Commonwealth Games comes to a close on home soil?
fullText:
How does a country define success at a Commonwealth Games?

Is it simply in the weight of medals? Does the colour come into it too?

Or is it in athletes reaching their own Everest? In doing themselves justice, making people proud and creating memories?

If it is numbers, those have proved encouraging for Team Scotland at their second home Games in 12 years. The bare statistics say Glasgow 2026 was Scotland's third best ever in terms of medals won.

They finished with 39 in total, including 13 golds - a mark bettered only by the 19 won at Glasgow 2014. Add nine silver and 17 bronze and they end up fifth in the medal table.

That's one place higher than Birmingham four years ago and with the same number of golds won.

But what is the detail hidden beneath those headlines? BBC Scotland has delved deeper into the results of 11 days of competition to try to find out...

Selfies, signatures & social media - how Kerr embraced Glasgow Games

Fachie survives painful crash to take another gold after Wales 'poke bear'

Very well. Granted, the overall haul and tally of golds sits some way shy of the last time in Glasgow, but it is worth considering a few factors before making such a crude determination.

Obviously, being at home was significant, but 2014 also had the largest number of athletes Scotland has ever had at a Games with 313.

Lop 130-odd off that for this time and the pitch is suddenly skewed.

Also consider that there were 261 golds available 12 years ago. In Birmingham, it was 283. This time, just 215 due to the streamlined sports programme.

That rationalisation means fewer athletes competing - 177 in Team Scotland this time, as compared to 261 in England. So a medal for every 4.54 competitors.

Given that figure was 5.30 four years ago, that could be considered progress.

Chef de mission Elinor Middlemiss steadfastly refused to state a medal target pre-Games - a caution perhaps founded in appreciating the narrow margins involved.

Take Duncan Scott. Scotland's most decorated Games athlete added two medals to his tally but had four fourth places and a fifth. On another day, any of those might have been rewarded with another slab of metal.

The swimmers were among a rash of fourth-place finishes for Scottish athletes, some by the most agonisingly narrow of margins.

A different bounce, step or lunge might have elevated those to medal-winning performances, just as it might have done for the athletes who came fifth or even sixth in their events.

"This has been a fantastic Games for Team Scotland and everyone connected with the team should feel immensely proud," Middlemiss said.

"Our athletes have delivered on so many fronts for the country: winning a plethora of medals, historic firsts, individual and team records and creating memories that will last a lifetime."

Yes, there was. Both in terms of different sports, genders and abilities.

Of the 10 different disciplines, only two failed to yield medals - netball and Para-powerlifting.

Athletics can reflect on their second biggest haul in 44 years. Gymnastics can celebrate a first-ever men's all-around gold. And satisfaction can be taken from an all-time best of 14 Para-sport medals.

A first team sport medal came in 3x3 basketball, followed by a second on the same day. Plus a first-ever podium in women's boxing.

Boxing, bowls and judo might harbour regrets, though, after disappointing results.

Of the 39 Scotland medals, 20 were claimed by men, 17 by women, with two podiums for mixed teams.

And, just like in Birmingham, 43% of those medals went to female athletes.

Nobody got anywhere close to the six medals that Duncan Scott reaped in Birmingham, with even the swimmer himself having to settle for two this time.

The 29-year-old did nudge himself further clear as Scotland's most decorated Games athlete with 14 medals in total, but he trails behind Neil Fachie when it comes to gold medals.

The Para-cyclist - who had effectively retired from the sport - claimed two golds here to take his tally to seven - two clear of bowler Alex 'Tattie' Marshall.

There were eight other multiple medallists in Team Scotland.

Angharad Evans was the standout performer, with two individual golds and relay silver and bronze in the pool.

Fellow swimmers Keanna MacInnes (three silver and one bronze), Katie Shanahan (two silver) Stephen Clegg (gold and silver) also enjoyed repeat success.

Para-athlete Melanie Woods won two golds on the track - one of them twice - and closing ceremony flagbearer Reuben Ward took gold and silver in gymnastics.

And, at the velodrome, Erin Boothman claimed double cycling bronze and Fin Graham silver and bronze.

title: From European hopes to relegation form - will Moyes reignite Everton?
description: Everton competed for the European places before falling away last season. BBC Sport examines whether David Moyes is the right man to turn them around this term.
fullText:
For much of last season, Everton were looking up.

Loan signing Jack Grealish proved to be an instant hit. Fellow new arrival Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall was a reliable matchwinner. Strikers Thierno Barry and Beto had shrugged off early-season struggles to start scoring goals.

A 3-0 triumph against Chelsea on 21 March put Everton eighth in the Premier League, just three points off the Champions League places with seven games left.

Supporters were dreaming big. Instead, the team imploded.

Everton failed to win any of their remaining matches - the longest run without a victory since David Moyes returned for a second spell in charge of the Toffees in 2025.

A 2-2 draw at Brentford on 11 April sparked a decline in form over the remainder of the campaign that ranked Everton in the bottom three during that period.

They were one of only three teams to fail to win a match during this spell, along with relegated Burnley and Wolves.

Despite the drop off, Everton retained hopes of European football when they faced Sunderland in their final home match of 2025-26.

In his program notes, Everton CEO Angus Kinnear declared that he was "happily dissatisfied" with the campaign - an odd turn of phrase at a confusing moment that quickly soured after a 3-1 defeat.

Promoted Sunderland would go on to finish seventh and secure European football for the first time in 53 years.

The irony for Moyes is that Everton have finished 13th in both seasons since his return, but to very different receptions.

When he rejoined the club 18 months ago, the Toffees were one point above the relegation zone. They would go on to finish 23 points clear of the bottom three.

Everton then spent £97m before the 2025-26 campaign - a club record net outlay in a summer transfer window - to repeat the same finish having accrued one more point.

Former Everton midfielder Leon Osman believes after a chaotic period of financial breaches, points deductions and relegation battles, successive mid-table finishes demonstrate progress.

"When David Moyes first came in, we flew out the blocks and had a great start," he said. "That continued for well over a year before the first sort of low period, which was the end of last season.

"I still feel that we made progress last season, which is what we wanted, along with stability."

Moyes, 63, has spoken of the challenge of keeping up with the biggest spenders in the Premier League, with Everton ranking 15th of the current top-flight teams for net spend over the past five years.

Bournemouth, however, spent the least of any Premier League team last summer, making a profit of £81m from player sales, and still finished seven places higher in sixth. Brighton made a profit of £41m and finished eighth.

Moving to the state-of-the-art Hill Dickinson Stadium promised a new dawn but Everton's points-per-game tally of 1.2 at home last season was the lowest by any team to start life in a new stadium in the Premier League in the competition's history - in stark comparison to strong away form which ranked the Toffees in the top seven.

Osman believes Bournemouth and Brighton are "further along in their development" than an Everton side still adjusting to new surroundings after a tumultuous period, and that the loss of Grealish to injury in January was key.

Everton's win rate dropped from 45% and 1.6 points per game with Grealish to 22% and one point per game without him.

"David Moyes is an intense manager and by the end of the season, a small squad couldn't quite last," said the 45-year-old.

"Changes take time. No one is thinking about relegation which shows you what Moyes has done. He's got 12 months remaining and I'd expect him to see that out."

While the success of Bournemouth and Brighton has been built on impressive recruitment models, Everton's transfer strategy remains a work in progress.

Under previous owner Farhad Moshiri, eight players signed for at least £20m left for nothing.

Following several years of limited spending, nine players were then recruited by the Friedkin Group last summer, although a focus on youth has yet to bear fruit.

Grealish and Dewsbury-Hall have been successful but 20-year-old winger Tyler Dibling has started only six matches after costing £35m from Southampton.

Young left-back Adam Aznou, who joined from Bayern Munich last summer, is still awaiting his Premier League debut.

Striker Barry, 23, won more aerial duels than any other player in his first Premier League campaign but was inconsistent in front of goal.

Midfielder Merlin Rohl, 24, initially struggled for game time before impressing over four starts in May.

BBC Radio Merseyside reporter Giulia Bould says the influential Grealish is set to re-sign on loan towards the end of this window as he continues to rehabilitate from a stress fracture to his foot.

His wages, however, are expected to stick at about £200,000 per week.

Iliman Ndiaye, meanwhile, has been linked with a move to Saudia Arabia.

"I'd welcome Grealish back but only at a price that suits Everton," says Osman, who was given his Everton debut by Moyes during the manager's first spell in charge in 2003.

"Ndiaye, I'd hate to lose him. There may come a point that the price is right and Everton can reinvest in two or three players but I think they should do everything they can to keep him."

Losing elite quality without sensible reinvestment is not something Everton can afford with one of the Premier League's smaller squads.

Moyes used just 22 players in the top flight in 2025-26 - the lowest of any side - while 128 substitutions were at least six fewer than any other manager.

Everton continue to focus a significant slice of their recruitment on development players.

Central midfielder Hayden Hackney, 24, joined from Middlesbrough for £16.5m in July along with 20-year-old winger Tyrique George, who was signed from Chelsea for £18m having spent the second half of last season on loan at Everton.

The more experienced Celtic defender Alistair Johnston is the latest player linked with solving the problem position at right-back, while 32-year-old Arsenal midfielder Christian Norgaard is reportedly an imminent arrival.

The average age of signings in Moyes' second spell is under 24, including three players aged 20 or younger.

But players aged 21 or under featured for 1,088 minutes for the club last season, ranking Everton only 17th in the Premier League.

The departures of Seamus Coleman and Idrissa Gueye deprive Everton of more than 600 Premier League appearances - explaining the interest in Norgaard - while key midfielder James Garner is set to miss the start of the season following groin surgery.

As things stand, it leaves Moyes in the paradoxical position of being potentially reliant on younger players he appears more reluctant to trust.

"They need to show they're capable and deserve to play," added Osman.

"I'm hoping that a year in, understanding the demands that are required, players like Dibling and George will make that progression and then suddenly our squad looks more trustworthy."

title: Newcastle sign Braga keeper Hornicek for £25.7m
description: Newcastle United sign goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek from Braga for £25.7m.
fullText:
Newcastle United have signed goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek from Braga for £25.7m.

Although Newcastle had already brought in 20-year-old Ewen Jaouen from Reims this summer, the club had also been in the market for a more established number one.

Hornicek, 24, flew out to Newcastle's training camp in Spain at the weekend to finalise his move and sign a five-year contract after the club activated his release clause.

"The last few days have been an emotional rollercoaster from when I first heard about the move and now I'm so happy to be here," the Czech Republic international said.

"It's a brilliant opportunity in a new league, which I'm very excited about. From the very first moment I arrived here, I received a fantastic welcome and really felt the warmth of the club. Everyone has been brilliant in helping me settle in.

"I know Newcastle is a huge football city, with 52,000 fans at St James' Park creating an incredible atmosphere and pushing the team every game. I can't wait to play in front of them."

Newcastle had tracked Hornicek's progress as he kept seven clean sheets during Braga's run to the Europa League semi-finals last season, which was the most of any goalkeeper in the competition.

As well as attempting to keep the ball out of the net, Opta data revealed Hornicek ranked second for successful passes (846) and fourth for passing accuracy (75%) of goalkeepers in Portugal's top-flight last season.

Newcastle sporting director Ross Wilson said the 24-year-old's "progress in recent years has been remarkable".

"He has firmly established himself as one of Europe's top young goalkeepers," Wilson said.

"We knew there would be no shortage of clubs interested in acquiring Lukas this summer after everything he achieved last season, but it quickly became evident how keen he was to be a part of what we are building here."

A rebuild was always on the cards on Tyneside this summer, not least in the goalkeeping department.

Leaky Newcastle kept just eight clean sheets in the Premier League last season and conceded 55 goals, 15th overall with only relegated Burnley, West Ham and Wolves plus Leeds and Tottenham below them.

Newcastle's outfield players clearly did not offer enough protection, but goalkeeper Nick Pope made a handful of significant errors leading to goals while Aaron Ramsdale never fully convinced during his loan spell and has since returned to Southampton.

A new number one was therefore a priority and Newcastle have once again looked to the continent.

The club have mainly targeted players aged 20 and under from abroad, having already recruited Jaouen, Sean Steur, Bazoumana Toure and Aladji Bamba, so Hornicek will feel like something of an elder statesman in comparison.

But the Czech only made his breakthrough as a regular starter at Braga 18 months ago and will not have much time to prepare for the physicality of the Premier League.

Hornicek's stature will certainly help - he's 6ft 6in tall - and his ability to play out from the back will give this side something different as a new cycle begins under head coach Mattias Jaissle, whose appointment will soon be formally announced.

Challenging times ahead for Newcastle - Shearer

Newcastle captain Guimaraes expected to join Arsenal

title: Man Utd boss Skinner leaves role before WSL season
description: Manchester United manager Marc Skinner steps down from his position before the start of the Women's Super League season.
fullText:
Manchester United manager Marc Skinner has left his position by mutual consent before the start of the Women's Super League season.

The 43-year-old has been in charge of United for five years and led them to their first major trophy with victory in the Women's FA Cup final in 2024.

He helped them reach the Women's Champions League group stages for the first time last year, while they finished runners-up in three domestic cup finals.

Skinner's departure comes a month before the start of the season with United set to travel to London City Lionesses on 4 September (19:00 BST).

The former Birmingham City head coach has raised concerns over a lack of investment in the squad and United have had a quiet summer.

United have changed their recruitment approach this year, targeting younger players in the hope of securing sustainable, long-term success.

BBC Sport reported in July that the girls' academy would train at Carrington - the club's main training facility - this season.

However, supporters have grown frustrated at the lack of spending in the transfer window with rivals Manchester City, Arsenal and Chelsea adding to their squads.

London City Lionesses, who finished fifth last season, signed two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas, while Lyon defender Alice Sombath joined Tottenham.

It is understood the club and Skinner held discussions in the summer and a mutual agreement for his departure was reached.

Sources at the club say they are advanced in their search for a replacement with background checks on potential candidates already completed.

One of the key requirements for Skinner's replacement is a coach with a history of developing players.

Skinner's time at United has been full of ups and downs and he was never able to win over a passionate fanbase.

Criticism hit an all-time high in 2024 when supporters took banners to Leigh Sports Village calling for Skinner's sacking.

He replaced former England defender Casey Stoney in 2021, who quit over frustrations at a lack of investment from the club.

That is an issue that has raised its head continually throughout Skinner's reign as he often pointed to the lack of squad depth following defeats to top-three rivals.

United owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe faced backlash for his comments on the women's team and there was outrage at their training facilities in 2024, which Skinner defended at the time.

Skinner did not have the same resources compared with other managers in the WSL and a smaller playing budget but was able to disrupt the usual order, leading United to two top-three finishes during his five-year spell at the club.

That meant they qualified for the Champions League – only making it out of the qualifying rounds last year.

However, he has been criticised by supporters on many occasions for a lack of bravery in big matches, stubbornness with his team selection and fewer homegrown players progressing from the academy and into the first team.

Their failure to qualify for the Champions League this season impacted their transfer window and despite signing a new contract last year - which tied Skinner down until 2027, with the option of a further year - it felt like relationships were no longer harmonious.

While Skinner previously backed the club in the face of criticism, he challenged more last season on spending and it was clear he wanted more backing.

Find interviews and extra content from the Women's Super League and beyond on the Women's Football Weekly feed

Get the latest WSL news on our dedicated page

title: AI slop blocked a real $200K macOS flaw
description: Apple's bug bounty program is drowning in AI-generated bug reports. The company has capped submissions per researcher because fabricated reports are clogging the review pipeline. As a result, Italian startup Bynario was initially unable to report a serious macOS vulnerability worth up to $200,000 on the black market.
fullText:
AI as a cybersecurity risk, but not the way you'd think. Apple is capping the number of bug reports security researchers can submit and enforcing a 30-day cooldown period. A flood of low-quality, AI-generated reports with hallucinated vulnerabilities is clogging the review pipeline, the Financial Times reports. Researchers can request a higher quota.

The cap creates real security gaps: Italian startup Bynario used ChatGPT to find a serious macOS vulnerability that could give attackers full control over a machine but couldn't report it because Apple had blocked further submissions. CEO Alfredo Pesoli estimates the flaw's black-market value at $100,000 to $200,000. Apple has since reached out to Bynario.

Meanwhile, Apple itself is using AI from Anthropic and OpenAI to hunt for vulnerabilities, and its latest updates included five times as many fixes as usual. That raises the question whether bug bounty programs can survive long-term or whether big tech companies will handle vulnerability discovery on their own. Rafe Pilling of Sophos told the FT that bug bounty programs have gone from finding vulnerabilities to validating them "at machine speed."

title: English FA set to join Welsh in withdrawing support for Infantino
description: The English Football Association is set to write to Fifa president Gianni Infantino withdrawing its support amid the fallout from his scrapped plans to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions to private investors.
fullText:
The English Football Association is set to write to Fifa president Gianni Infantino withdrawing its support amid the fallout from his scrapped plans to sell off stakes in Fifa competitions to private investors.

It comes as Uefa threatens legal action over the proposals and Wales publicly withdraw backing for Infantino's bid to continue as Fifa president.

Infantino's leadership had already been publicly questioned by football's governing bodies in Europe, North and Central America and the Caribbean, with Uefa and Concacaf releasing statements criticising the plans.

Fifa and Infantino wanted to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including its World Cups, and external investors would have been able to buy stakes in it.

World football's governing body said it would "invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments" in a new subsidiary called Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE).

As first reported by The Telegraph, Uefa said in a letter to Infantino "it is actively considering legal action, arbitration, and/or regulatory complaints (together, the 'proceedings') arising out of and in connection with the FFE plan proposed by Fifa".

Uefa added it wants "immediate steps to identify, locate and preserve all documents and electronically stored information described in this notice that are in your or Fifa possession, custody or control.

"These obligations arise independently of any internal retention policy you or your organisation maintain and supersede any routine document destruction or deletion policies that would otherwise apply."

BBC Sport has approached Fifa for comment.

A bruising 24 hours - what next for Fifa and under-pressure Infantino?

Call for 'full review' as pressure grows on Infantino

Is Infantino finished? Could Uefa boycott World Cup? What happens now?

Infantino wrote to all 211 Fifa member associations saying they would receive $40m (£30m) if they backed his controversial proposal, setting a deadline of 19 September if they wanted to access an initial $20m (£15m).

Thrive Eternal was expected to lead the proposed investor group for FFE.

Thrive is an American venture capital firm founded by Joshua Kushner - the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared.

Uefa's request for all documents regarding the investment plan, included "email, instant messages (WhatsApp, Signal, Teams, Slack or any other platform), SMS, written correspondence and meeting notes", and those which involved "any Fifa officer, employee, committee member, consultant or agent, or any Fifa member association, confederation, broadcaster, sponsor, or financial institution".

In reference to the 19 September deadline, Uefa added it wanted documents to be retained "relating to the payment structure for Fifa member associations, including the design, modelling, legal basis, approval and communications to member associations".

Uefa asked Infantino to acknowledge receipt of its letter in writing within five business days, to confirm he had "received and understood this notice" and that he has "taken immediate steps to preserve relevant materials as required".

As the pressure grows on Infantino, Qatar, Lebanon, Kuwait and Sri Lanka have pledged their support for his Fifa leadership to continue.

If he holds out until March, he could stand for re-election for a fourth and final term as president and would need 106 votes from Fifa's 211 members to win.

Uefa has 55 votes, Africa 54, Asia 46, Concacaf 35, Oceania 11 and Conmebol 10.

The Asian Football Federation (AFC) has said it stands in "solidarity" with Uefa and Concacaf, while Africa, Conmebol and Oceania have not criticised Infantino's plan.

However, the Fifa Council could try to force Infantino to resign through an emergency meeting.

That would be triggered if 19 of the 37 Fifa Council members call for one and the meeting must take place within two weeks.

Uefa has nine members, AFC has seven, Concacaf five, Africa has six, Conmebol five and Oceania three. It is completed by Infantino and secretary general Mattias Grafstrom.

This heaps yet more pressure on the beleaguered Fifa president Gianni Infantino, and is further evidence that the revolt against him over the FFE saga is being driven by Uefa.

The demand that senior Fifa officials do not destroy any evidence relevant to the scrapped plans to sell off stakes in its competitions will be uncomfortable for those named in the letter, and represents a further escalation in the feud between the two organisations.

It remains uncertain whether the threat of legal action - and European member associations withdrawing previous letters of support - is enough for Infantino to consider his position and step down.

But, if not, Uefa will hope it at least helps to secure the 19 votes needed (of 37) to force an emergency meeting of the Fifa Council at which Infantino could face a demand to step down.

A motion to call one will not be submitted until they are certain they have the required numbers, but that could be where this dramatic story is heading next.

The situation is delicately poised. Uefa knows it has to be avoid being perceived as telling the rest of the world what to do, and it is clear that Infantino retains considerable support outside Europe and the Concacaf region.

Opposition from just those two confederations is unlikely to be enough to unseat him, and so efforts are currently being made behind the scenes to convince countries elsewhere to join the rebellion.
