title: Day to remember for record-breaking Finucane
description: Emma Finucane creates history by winning a fourth track cycling Commonwealth Games gold and leads Wales into closing ceremony.
fullText:
Not many top sports stars have perfect days during their career.

Creating history by winning a fourth track cycling Commonwealth gold in one Games and leading your nation into the closing ceremony will come close for Wales' Emma Finucane.

The 23-year-old from Carmarthen started the day at 9am in the first heat of the keirin.

Twelve hours later and having emphatically claimed the gold on the final day of competition, Finucane was tasked with carrying the Welsh flag as Glasgow closed the Games.

"I don't think I'll ever believe I've created history here and I can't believe little me has done this," said Finucane.

"The 10-year-old Emma is screaming inside about what is going on. I don't think it'll sink in probably until the next Commonwealth Games."

'A huge success' - Wales win 31 medals at Glasgow Games

Finucane creates Games history with fourth gold

Team Wales roll of honour at Commonwealth Games

The 23-year-old's fantastic four gold medals on the track in one Commonwealth Games has not been done before. By anybody in any velodrome.

This was in not just any old velodrome. It was the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome. The Scottish legend who is considered one of the finest track sprinters in history.

But Sir Chris did not win four Commonwealth titles at one Games. Nor did Victoria Pendleton, Jason Kenny, Becky North or Anna Meares.

Wales' own golden girl now has, but the rider herself would not comprehend the comparisons.

"No, I'm nowhere near them," said Finucane.

"They are icons of the sport. Absolute legends. To even have my name beside them is insane.

"I am not in their class but it's something you don't think about as an athlete. We're in a little bubble in here.

"I am going to keep doing what I'm doing, go out there and ride with passion and love and see how far I can go in the sport."

Finucane has already gone pretty far probably considering she was already an Olympic champion at 21 and has achieved this remarkable feat in Glasgow at 23.

Pressure was on her this week to achieve the four golds because she was an obvious class apart from the field. Even a field that included triple Olympic champion Ellesse Andrews.

After winning the team sprint with Rhian Edmunds and Lowri Thomas, Finucane was imperious with stunning success in the individual sprint, 1,000m time trial and keirin.

Her physical prowess is there for everybody to see but her mental capability has also stood up to the test over four remarkable days.

"I definitely felt the pressure," said Finucane.

"Throughout the week, I just rode for my own race and it unfolded how it did.

"After yesterday, the media were asking can you do four? I wanted to and knew it might be possible.

"In that semi-final I nearly didn't get through so I just enjoyed that final. I wanted to ride a race I was proud of.

"I rode it with confidence. I got myself to the front and just went out there and left everything on the track."

Finucane has also created history in her own country by becoming the most successful Welsh woman in Games history.

The honour of representing Wales is important to her as Finucane normally competes for Great Britain in major events like the Olympics and world championships.

Finucane revealed she has been inspired by a speech by her Welsh team-mate Lewis Oliva on what it meant to represent the nation.

"I was crying my eyes out when I heard this," said Finucane.

"He said this was the reason we do what we do, because you are Welsh.

"He ignited a fire in me. I was determined to ride for Wales and was going to do it with passion."

It worked as Finucane led a Welsh cycling medal charge in Glasgow with 11 podium positions.

This included six gold, three silver and two bronze, the most successful Commonwealth return for the sport.

Finucane has heard the Welsh anthem four times in successive days, once with two team-mates and three on her own.

She was the most emotional for this final one as she came to terms with what she had achieved.

"I was an absolute mess on the podium," said Finucane.

"I saw my family in front of me, the Welsh flag, and then all my team-mates also draped in the red flag.

"Things like this happen once every four years and I wanted to stand on that top set, sing the anthem and live in the moment."

Finucane was not the only one who was a mess.

In the crowd, her sister was in tears at the anthem alongside her parents, while her boyfriend Matthew Richardson was in contact from Japan.

The cyclist was due to compete for England before getting injured in a cycling crash, something else Finucane has had to deal with.

She says she is backed up by her family support.

"My mum and dad, my sister and partner was here, my brother's back at home and Matty was on FaceTime," said Finucane.

"He's literally in Japan and it's like 2am and he's called me.

"So I have a massive support network network with me and they love me no matter what.

"They'll text me, if you win or lose and that means everything because they don't put stress on me."

Having conquered the Commonwealth, Finucane was asked whether her attention will turn to the Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028.

"I knew these questions would come, but I want to live in the moment," said Finucane.

"It's something I haven't been good at in the past. I've been always been looking at the next challenge.

"I have the World Championships in 10 weeks. I'm actually going away on holiday with on my sister and then I'll reset for them.

"But for now I'll just soak it in and it probably won't do that for a long time."

The short-term was more pressing because Finucane had somewhere to be as she was whisked off to prepare for the closing ceremony.

During the numerous interviews she conducted after the race, Finucane was told in one by Team Wales chef de mission Gethin Jones she would be the flag bearer.

"I'm so honoured and I'm going to wave that flag with so much pride because Wales is amazing," said Finucane.

"It's such a beautiful place. We have so much pride, so much passion and so much talent.

"I feel like I'm living in an absolute dream. I can't believe I'm going to be the one standing there on television with the flag. It just doesn't feel real, it probably never will.

"I want to live in that moment, just breathe, realise what I'm doing, and fly the flag as loud and as proudly as I can."

title: Kuwaki wins Women's Open after Henseleit's ball strikes marshal
description: Shiho Kuwaki holds her nerve to beat Esther Henseleit after two play-off holes to become the second consecutive Japanese player to win the Women's Open.
fullText:
AIG Women's Open - fourth round

-5 *S Kuwaki (Jap), E Henseleit (Ger); -4 Y Noh (US); -2 N Korda (US), J Thitikul (Tha)

Selected others: -1 C Hull (Eng), L Woad, (Eng), H Ryu (Kor), R Takeda (Jap); E C Boutier (Fra), S Kouskova (Cze); +1 L Li (US), L Coughlin (US)

Shino Kuwaki won the Women's Open in dramatic fashion after an extraordinary play-off in which Esther Henseleit's hopes were hit by her ball taking an unfortunate ricochet off a marshal.

The gripping finale at Royal Lytham & St Annes brimmed with drama, magic and misfortune - particularly on the crucial 18th hole.

Germany's Henseleit initially forced an extension to play by sinking a 45-foot birdie putt to draw level at five under par with Japan's Kuwaki, who sat nervously inside the clubhouse watching on.

However, after both made pars in distinctly different fashion on the first sudden-death play-off hole, Henseleit was left in difficulty when her drive hit a course marshal and was redirected into a gorse bush as they went down the 18th for a third time.

When she was unable to save her par, it was left for Kuwaki to make a short putt for a four to secure the top prize of £1.11m just 12 months after failing to make the cut at Royal Porthcawl.

"I just can't believe it," said Kuwaki, whose previous five wins as a professional had all arrived on her home tour.

"To be on a stage like this is an honour and every hole I was just focused on shot by shot. I just tried to enjoy it as much as I could.

"It's an amazing feeling to win again as a Japanese player. I hope as team Japan we can continue to light up the golf world."

For most of Sunday afternoon the most pertinent question appeared to be if anyone could catch the unfancied Yealimi Noh.

And if so, just who, on a day when the vagaries of links golf on the blustery Lancashire coast propelled several players into realistic contention and just as quickly swept their aspirations aside.

Unfortunately for world number 69 Noh, that included her hopes of claiming just her second ever win on the professional circuit as she finished a stroke back.

Instead, Kuwaki - the only player in the final eight groups to go under par on the day along with Henseleit - provided the answer and in the end was a deserved winner despite her play-off opponent's misfortune.

Henseleit had been aiming to follow in Sophia Popov's footsteps by becoming only the second German female to win a major, and her heroics on the 18th green as she concluded her round with Noh postponed Kuwaki's celebrations for almost an hour.

Prior to that Kuwaki's one-under 70 had put her in prime position to become the fourth Japanese to win the tournament.

The English challenge of Lottie Woad and Charley Hull had failed to spark while Haeran Ryu's ability to contend had been hampered by her frequent trips into the bunkers festooned around Royal Lytham & St Annes.

And world number one Nelly Korda was left rueing her double-bogey finish in Saturday's third round, that frustratingly put her just out of reach of a career grand slam 24 hours later, despite carding a three-under 68 to end the championship at two under.

For a time as the early-evening chill began to factor, Henseleit's steady approach threatened to deliver the ultimate dividend.

The 27-year-old recovered from successive bogeys on the eighth and ninth holes to birdie the 11th, 12th and 15th, before the pressure told on the 16th green and a left-to-right putt lacking conviction slid past the edge of the cup to deliver a costly bogey.

However, to her credit she regrouped and set up a superb climax with a magical moment before a packed gallery in front of the clubhouse.

"It was a great moment when that putt dropped in," said Henseleit, who will feature for Europe at the Solheim Cup in September.

"Very happy with how I gave myself the opportunity to win today and how I handled myself. Just got a bit unlucky on the second play-off hole there."

However, Kuwaki more than merited her celebrations in the fading daylight, not that you could have missed her with her mint-green top and luminous green ball.

And she matched her eye-catching fashion sense with a similar performance from tee to green, carving out several excellent birdie chances that could have provided her with a more comfortable Sunday evening.

Her birdie on the 13th arrived as Noh was in a spot of bother on the 12th having pushed a birdie chance way past its intended target.

And while the American, who ended up carding a bogey, immediately bounced back a further dropped shot on the 14th signalled that it would not be her day.

While her second appearance in September's Solheim Cup match against Europe now seems assured, for the 25-year-old it will come as scant consolation.

While Kuwaki becomes the 43rd different winner in 50 editions of the Women's Open, Noh is the first to have held a three-stroke lead after 54 holes and failed to win the championship.

title: Tale of two halves leaves Iraola with plenty to ponder
description: On the overnight flight from Chicago back to England, Andoni Iraola will have plenty of thinking to do after the conclusion of Liverpool's pre-season US tour.
fullText:
On the flight home from Chicago, as he reflects on the 4-2 loss to Leeds that ended Liverpool's United States tour, manager Andoni Iraola will have plenty to think about.

The first-half display was arguably the best since the Spaniard took charge, but the second was categorically their worst as they conceded four times without reply inside 25 minutes.

Iraola did make a raft of changes at the break and in the second half but that is no excuse for the way they capitulated against Daniel Farke's side.

Their lack of squad depth and physicality was alarmingly exposed and Iraola will be concerned with the ease with which Leeds scored, albeit against an inexperienced backline that finished with Calvin Ramsay, Ifeanyi Ndukwe and Mor Talla Ndiaye.

With Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz making their return, Liverpool were excellent in the first half and it is important not to be too critical but perhaps Iraola will be glad in the long-run that he saw this second-half display, where Liverpool's set-piece deficiencies were evident too.

"We conceded two goals from set-pieces. We have to fix that and make sure we deal with them better," said midfielder Dominik Szoboszlai.

The intensity Iraola demands on the training pitch was evident in the first half but seemed non-existent after the break. Senior figures like Curtis Jones and Federico Chiesa did not cover themselves in glory.

"I particularly hate this month of August because you start the competitions and you still don't know if some of the players are going to leave and who's going to come - there is a lot of uncertainty," said Iraola, earlier in the week.

Iraola will meet Virgil van Dijk, Cody Gakpo, Alisson Becker and new signing Victor Munoz over the coming days at the AXA Training Centre.

However, over the course of a fortnight in America, Liverpool have had no incomings. That was in part because Iraola wanted to see the squad at his disposal before making decisions.

What he saw in this defeat will play into those decisions.

Even before the second-half troubles, Iraola would have known that there was no time to waste as he plans for the start of the season, his starting 11 reflecting this with Isak and Wirtz in against Leeds - even if the state of the pitch suggested that could be a risk.

The inclusion of a pair who cost a combined £225m last summer also gave the teamsheet the star quality befitting the host city of Chicago, home to both the Lollapalooza Festival and Major League Baseball series between the New York Yankees and the Chicago Cubs over the weekend.

And in what was Liverpool's best half of the tour, Isak looked sharp and Wirtz scored as they suffocated Leeds with their press and moved the ball around with confidence.

Their early breakthrough came from an unlikely source. Luke Chambers spent the second half of last season on loan at Charlton Athletic but, given Liverpool's centre-half crisis, the left-back moved inside against Wrexham in Liverpool's previous friendly and kept his place.

Fresh from impressing Iraola in New York, Chambers hammered home from inside the box in the seventh minute after Milos Kerkez got a touch on Szoboszlai's corner.

Rio Ngumoha caused havoc down his preferred left flank while 19-year-old Trey Nyoni continued his excellent pre-season with another solid showing. In the 40th minute, he floated a ball across to Jeremie Frimpong, who cut it back to Wirtz and the German did the rest. It was a wonderful team goal that involved Isak too.

Nyoni has been linked with a loan move this summer but on these showings, the midfielder will surely stay and get more minutes for Liverpool this season.

He only played 229 minutes in 2025-26 but Iraola has spoken glowingly about his attributes, not least his confidence on the ball and his desire to go direct.

title: 'No guarantees' - joyful Glasgow cannot banish all Commonwealth doubts
description: Glasgow 2026 was a joyful success in isolation but questions and doubts remain about the Commonwealth Games' future.
fullText:
Glasgow has performed the surgery the Commonwealth Games needed to keep it alive.

Eleven days. 674 medals. Thousands of happy fans.

But this is only the start of the recovery.

The Indian city of Ahmedabad now stands where Victoria did four years ago - as the next hosts of an event that will celebrate its 100th anniversary in 2030.

Victoria pulled out. Can Ahmedabad give certainty it won't?

"I don't think one can give any guarantees," Raghu Iyer - chief executive of the Indian Olympic Association - told BBC Sport.

It was a note of caution that showed questions about the Games' future had not been banished as the 2026 Games closed on Sunday evening.

Why the Commonwealth Games are important to NI athletes

'A huge success' - Wales win 31 medals at Glasgow Games

After Victoria withdrew in 2023, Glasgow answered the SOS call - and organisers say the past 11 days in the Scottish city have "exceeded all expectations".

Yes, there have been grumbles - including from those who have seen parking spaces outside their houses taken - and taxi drivers and shop owners the Games have passed by.

On the ground, though, this felt like a meaningful event.

Ticket sales of 434,000 were well down from 1.5 million for Birmingham 2022, but they were always going to be given the smaller venues for this scaled-back edition. It has been rare to enter a venue and not find a joyful, engaged crowd.

There was plenty of excitement for fans, too - Josh Kerr's golden homecoming at Scotstoun, Angharad Evans making the swimming pool floors shake, and Neil Fachie's emotional victory on his return to the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.

They also celebrated Jamaica's seismic netball win over Australia. Live sport rarely fails to deliver.

But a nagging question has remained throughout: is anyone else watching?

Big names such as Kerr and Adam Ramsay-Peaty - with his emotional reaction to taking bronze in the pool - broke out of this Glaswegian bubble, but what else?

Organisers said their social media views passed those of Birmingham within the opening few days and highlighted record-breaking television figures in Australia and New Zealand, where the Games were free-to-air.

Still, without that same coverage in the UK, these Games have - at times - drifted by.

Glasgow 2026 was also hurt by the absence or late withdrawal of big-name competitors, particularly in athletics, which missed Keely Hodgkinson, Katarina Johnson-Thompson and Dina Asher-Smith.

The Games' differing relevance between sports was again clear - for netball, this remains the pinnacle and is treated as such; for others, it is a stepping stone. Many narratives focused on the "next generation".

Eighteen-year-old Jersey swimmer Filip Nowacki was perhaps the most exciting name to emerge, but gymnasts Ruby Evans (Wales) and Reuben Ward (Scotland) and England track cyclist Henry Hobbs, who won two golds and a bronze, were others.

Swimmer Faye Rogers impressively brought her success at the Paralympics back to Glasgow with gold in the pool - and then competed in the non-para event as well.

Cyclist Emma Finucane turned her three Olympic medals in Paris into four Commonwealth golds in Glasgow.

All will have their eyes on Los Angeles in 2028.

But what does this all mean for the future of the Commonwealth Games?

A move to October for Ahmedabad will free athletics from a scheduling tussle with the European Championships. It will, though, extend a gruelling season and give athletes a different decision to make.

That the next Games are seen as a step towards India hosting the Olympics and Paralympics - possibly also in Ahmedabad - should help ensure their success.

The main venue will be the 120,000-seater cricket stadium which bears the name of Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

Given the issues at Delhi 2010, plenty will be watching with interest.

But as the number of sports rises - not beyond 20, as was planned for Victoria, but to 17 from the 10 in Glasgow - so will costs.

They were slashed from £800m here, but the budget for Ahmedabad 2030 is almost double Glasgow's £160m. Therein lies a conflict.

This version has been billed as a template for the future, but immediately there is change. A financial and logistical circle needs to be squared.

The specific sports returning for Ahmedabad will be interesting too.

While the Olympics have recently added skateboarding, surfing and breakdancing, the Commonwealths - with India having a big say - look set to reintroduce cricket, shooting, archery and hockey.

Cricket, though, would be another sport for which this event does not represent the biggest prize.

The BBC has been invited back to the negotiating table for broadcast rights, too.

But perhaps most significant is the fact sports, nations and thousands of athletes still want to be here - each for many different reasons.

"I always looked up to it as a little girl and wanted to compete at a Commonwealth Games," said 5,000m runner Rose Davies - part of the Australia squad that won 70 of the 216 golds.

"It is a big part of our development and one of the goals an athlete has."

Tarona Taafaki looked more broadly after winning Tuvalu's first Commonwealth medal.

"It means there's a start, there's a beginning, and right now it just the beginning of what Tuvalu can reach in the future," she said.

If that drive remains, so will hope for the future.

title: Irish boxer Reeves 'critical but stable' in hospital
description: Irish boxer Lee Reeves is in a "critical but stable" condition in hospital after he was stretchered out of the ring in Dublin on Saturday.
fullText:
Irish boxer Lee Reeves is in a "critical but stable" condition in hospital after he was stretchered out of the ring in Dublin on Saturday.

Reeves was facing Gary Cully for the vacant BUI Celtic super-lightweight title but was knocked out in the 10th round at the 3Arena.

The 31-year-old Limerick fighter was stretchered out of the ring after the fight and transferred to hospital.

In an update released on Sunday, a spokesperson from Queensberry Promotions said that Reeves is in a "critical but stable" condition.

"Lee Reeves is still in hospital, in a critical but stable condition," the spokesperson said.

"We will know 

Speaking after the fight, Cully said that his "prayers and thoughts" were with Reeves.

"Hopefully he's okay," said Cully.

"He came in there as a big underdog after fighting relatively at a lower level up until now, but he really showed that he can operate at a higher level. Huge credit to him."

In a social media post after the fight, Queensberry promoter Frank Warren said his "thoughts and prayers" were with Reeves and his family.

"Everyone at Queensberry is thinking of him and we're in constant contact with his team regarding his condition as we hope for positive news," he said.

The bout was taking place on the undercard of Pierce O'Leary against Mark Chamberlain, which the home fighter lost via knockout in the 10th round.
